recipes.name: Grandma’s Cornbread Dressing
ingredients_raw: 1 tablespoon dried sage, or more to taste
salt and ground black pepper to taste

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease a 7x11-inch baking dish. Place crumbled cornbread in a large bowl.
Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add onion and celery and sauté until soft, 5 to 7 minutes.

Add sautéed onion and celery to the crumbled cornbread. Stir in eggs, sage, salt, and pepper. Gradually stir in chicken stock until the cornbread is evenly moistened. Transfer to the prepared baking dish.
Bake in the preheated oven until the dressing is lightly golden around the edges and the center reaches 165 degrees F (74 degrees C), about 30 minutes.

raw_recipe.headline: Grandma’s Cornbread Dressing
raw_recipe.description: This old-fashioned cornbread dressing combines crumbled cornbread, onion, celery, sage, and chicken stock for a savory Thanksgiving side.

video.description: In this video, Nicole shows you how to make Grandma's Cornbread Dressing.

review.reviewBody: This is an excellent recipe if you are familiar with southern cornbread but never cooked it and want to try with a basic recipe. If you are new to making it, some things you DEFINITELY need to know: 1)"Dry Corn Bread Mix" is "corn meal mix" with the baking powder and flour already in it, and not Jiffy or sweet brands. The Aunt Jemima, Martha White or White Lily brands are perfect. Sweet dressing doesn't have the traditional southern taste. 2)Sage is delicious but it is VERY strong. If you are not used to sage, cut the recipe amount in half and add your sage to the recipe before the eggs, so you can taste as you go along. 3)The more you stir and mix this recipe, the more dense and gummier it gets. If its "wet" before you bake it, the stiffer it will be when it's done. It will sit up like a brick! If you like a lighter, fluffier dressing ("stuffing" like), only add as much liquid as needed to be visibly moist like thick stew; it should still be chunky when you pour it in the baking dish to get a light consistency. 4)For non-vegetarians, add meat to this dish! Almost any meat will go well: cubed or shredded turkey, ham, chicken, sausage, ground beef, bacon. Try your favorite. 5)BE CAREFUL if you use poultry seasoning, some blends have salt. Reduce the recipe salt if needed. 6) My grandma told me her secret to good dressing is the vegetables, so use plenty celery & onion. Cook them only until tender and the onions are translucent so you don't lose all the crunch. It adds great t

I made a few modifications to make it more like my Grandma's recipe - increased celery to 1 cup, added 3/4 cup chopped bell pepper, 1/2 tsp. poultry seasoning + large pinch of sage, 1 tsp. salt, 1/2 tsp. pepper, and used the entire mix of cornbread instead of 3 cups as it says (Jiffy brand comes in 8 1/2 oz. boxes - use 2 boxes). Wow, what a hit with my crowd! I found it easy to bake it for 30 minutes the night before, refrigerate, let it come to room temperature, then bake it 10-15 minutes before serving is perfect. Thanks for the recipe!

If you add the sage to the chicken stock and warm the liquid up, it helps tremendously with the sage distribution. Therefore you won't feel you have to add more or maybe use less ( depending on your taste). I also add green pepper to the sauté.... It's what we call the holy trinity of cooking. I also add cream of muchroom and chicken soup to the mixture as well as prepackged breadcrubs... For added texture I boil the innards of the turkey ( or chicken) with the stock and use the extra meat inside the dressing. Oh yeah, when my mom taught me to make this she told me to make sure the cornbread baked long enough for the bottom to turn at least medium brown.

This is pretty much how I make my dressing however, I fried 2 strips of bacon, then cooked my onions, celery & 2 small chopped carrots in the bacon grease. I added all that to my dressing mix. I also added one T of achiote & cilantro (optional) , one can of diced chicken, one can of cream of chicken soup, one can of chicken broth and 1/2 cup of milk to reach the consistency I wanted. I sprayed my casserole dish with butter.

I have bunches of food allergies sensitivities, so I change almost every recipe. I used half a batch of my favorite cornbread. (GF Corn meal and no flour, Oat milk and no dairy....) I dropped the celery (doesn't agree with me) and increased the onion. Did it call for garlic? Plenty of garlic. I sautéed it in olive oil, since butter is out. Because store bought broth contains problem ingredients, I made a little stock by boiling the turkey neck with a few seasonings and used that for the stock. I chose to bake mine in the same cast iron pan I use to bake cornbread. I am very happy with how it came out. I just wish I could have made more. I have a big pot of stock going from the bones and back. I can make more soon if I want to!

Very close to what I grew up with in Louisiana! I use 5 cups of cornbread to use up the rest of the cornbread in the skillet. I added two diced boiled eggs and three stalks of diced green onion to mine, and an extra cup and a half of broth. We always liked our dressing a little bit looser than conventional dressing, and this was a great starter recipe to tweak until I get it just the way it was when I was a kid.

Its the same I learned except you bake the cornbread on Monday and let it sit out. Also cook a lb of sausage and add it with a bag of Pepperidge Farm dressing mix. Takes slot of sage and at least a cube of better to cook onions and celery in.

I also bake my Cornbread with Jiffy,I use all ingredients mentioned in recipe, onion,celery,bell peppers , sage,Buttery Poultry blend ,light salt & pepper, of course my chicken broth or stock after I shred Tysons Grilled chicken strips, my mom cooked all her dishes with everything homemade, I take short cuts, My mom taught me how to cook, what spices/seasonings to use when cooking, I mix it all in bowl then I pour it into large speckled baking pan with a lid, photo above, my mom had a huge baking pan,we have a big family so therefore, everything was huge, I'm going to use this recipe, for Christmas Dinner, Thanksgiving Cornbread Dressing was good, but, this one is going to top that one..

FOR GLUTEN-FREE PEOPLE -- This recipe will be the foundation for making a gluten-free version for my dear son, who really misses the old gluten-loaded Thanksgivings of his youth! [And I agree, the dressing is the truly fragrant essence of the holiday!] I make gluten-free cornbread using a cup of Bob's Red Mill 1-to-1 Gluten-Free (instead of AP white flour) with the recipe on Indian Head brand stone-ground cornmeal (yellow or white). Tastes great. Another hint I haven't seen anywhere else: I add half a can of creamed corn to the batter (reduce the milk and oil a bit to allow for the extra moisture) and it makes the bread even better.

This recipe is pretty much the same as what l grew up with and make now. Difference is, l usually cook breakfast for everyone that morning and all leftovers is tossed into the dressing. Whether it be eggs, bacon, sausage or biscuits, Grandma taught me not to waste anything. l do use the water l boil the innards of the turkey in. And even chop some of the liver, gizzard, and neckmeat in dressing and turkey gravy. Even my pup gets a treat with the liver also. All fed and happy
Two cups of chicken stock is way too much. I used 1/2 cup and it was plenty moist, and my cornbread was not dry. I will use this recipe again when we have leftover cornbread, but with modifications.

I noticed that the original recipe called for two tablespoons of sage and this was ready to one based on feedback. I used 2.5 tablespoons and it’s just like my Southern grandmother’s dressing. We’re never really measured so I was looking for general guidance. I used way more than two cups of stock, more like 3. We always made it so it looked like loose cornbread batter so it wouldn’t be dry. The sage profile changes after cooked so we also went heavy on the sage. We made sure we were happy with the taste before adding the eggs. Great recipe to start with.
This looks delicious and thank you for posting it.

My Mother from down south used to divide off about a 1/4 section with a strip of foil where she’d add in some Red Pepper Spice for those who wanted a little zip! Also, she’d add in some turkey meat as others have suggested. She never used bell pepper — only onion & celery. And she’d use a mixture of cornbread, white bread, and canned biscuits w/milk and chicken broth. Everyone loved her cornbread dressing. 💗
nice thanksgiving turkey side

This recipe is similar to my mom’s. I make my own cornbread. When adding ingredients to my baked, crumbled cornbread, I don’t use sage or raw eggs. I add a little olive oil, maybe a tablespoon and sometimes I add a couple of diced boiled eggs, as well as 2 cans of Campbell’s condensed chicken noodle soup. I add chicken broth as I’m mixing until I get the right consistency, then add salt, if needed and always pepper to taste. If you don’t already have a meat, you can add diced chicken thighs or chicken breast while mixing. Bake 45 minutes at 400 degrees.
Only change, no celery. My forever recipe!
This is just like my grandma’s dressing. I do add a box of stuffing to it.

I made this a few months ago for Thanksgiving and my guy was begging me to make it again the following week. I've made it several more times since then. I love how easy it is to tweak the recipe and make it your own. I made it the other day, but added a 3rd egg. I sauted carrots along with the onions. And added diced ham, making it more like a casserole kind of dish. It was delicious!

This was okay. The flavor was fine. I may not have crumbled the cornbread as much as I should have. It seemed to be missing body from the cornbread. It certainly wasn't my Mom's dressing. Perhaps I was hoping it might have or could have been like her's.
